bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Genuinely national delivery footprint: Integrated Facility Management deploys approximately 55,000 people across all 28 states and 5 UTs and contributed around 49% of total revenue in FY26
- Integrated single-accountability model across soft, technical and allied services, food, industrial O&M, telecom, security and talent — clients increasingly buy integrated solutions rather than standalone services, making the Company a strategic partner
- Client stickiness: 95% client retention in FY26 across more than 1,000 organisations spanning ten sectors
- Compliance and safety record described as mattering enormously in regulated sectors, where Bluspring has built a reputation
- Technology visibility for clients — real-time dashboards, automated compliance tracking and predictive capabilities replacing monthly reporting with continuous live visibility
- Independent service-quality recognition: a major international airport under management was named Cleanest Airport in India and South Asia (under-five-million-passenger category) at the Skytrax World Airport Awards 2026, retaining the title for a second consecutive year
- Scale of workforce — more than 93,000 colleagues (Chairman's message)
- Structural tailwind alignment: formalisation of the workforce (four Labour Codes in force 21 November 2025; ELI Scheme with ₹99,446 crore outlay), rising outsourcing intensity, technology enablement and ESG-linked contracting all favour organised, compliant providers
- Large headroom in food and catering — the business's share of the organised B2B catering market stands at slightly over 1%
- Fitch credit rating secured during the year, which further reduced borrowing costs
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Workforce management risk — recruiting, training and retaining qualified personnel; high attrition — Bluspring is a people-intensive, multi-site service business managing roughly 93,000 people across client sites, so difficulty in recruiting, training and retaining qualified personnel, or high attrition rates, could disrupt operations and increase costs. Mitigations stated: investment in a robust people supply chain backed by recruitment, onboarding and training programmes; benchmarked compensation models and focused retention strategies to reduce attrition and ensure operational continuity.
- Working capital and cash flow risk — Negative cash flows and working capital requirements can impact operations and the ability to meet short-term obligations — structurally acute in an outsourced services model where wages are paid ahead of client collections. Mitigations stated: diversified revenue streams across multiple service lines to reduce dependency on any single vertical; tightly managed collections and credit control; prioritising cash-generating contracts and segments; and strategic partnerships to optimise working capital cycles.
- Labour law compliance risk across multiple states — Stringent labour regulations and compliance requirements across multiple states carry potential penalties for non-compliance. This is doubly structural for Bluspring: the four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, and the report elsewhere attributes the year's exceptional items primarily to the estimated one-time impact of adopting the new labour code (higher provision towards retiral benefits) — so the same regulation is both the Company's tailwind and its largest compliance exposure. Mitigations stated: in-house legal and compliance teams enforcing standardised processes, regular field-team training on labour law updates, and proactive engagement with regulatory authorities.
- Regulatory and licensing risk — suspension or non-renewal of critical permits — Multiple licences and approvals are required across the different business verticals (facility management, catering, security, telecom, industrial O&M), and suspension or non-renewal of a critical permit would halt delivery. Mitigations stated: a centralised regulatory tracking system with domain-specific legal expertise per vertical; proactive application, timely renewal and close monitoring of all statutory licences; periodic internal compliance audits; and maintenance of all critical certifications including ISO, PSARA and OHSAS to meet client and regulatory expectations.
- Data privacy and cybersecurity risk, including DPDP Act 2023 compliance — Risks related to data breaches, cyber-attacks and non-compliance with evolving data protection regulations including the DPDP Act 2023 — material given the Company runs digital workforce, attendance and billing platforms and a talent marketplace holding job-seeker data. Mitigations stated: a data protection framework aligned with the IT Act, Privacy Rules and the DPDP Act; continuous strengthening of security infrastructure through regular audits and timely system upgrades; and periodic employee training on data privacy and cybersecurity protocols.
- Food safety and quality risk in the catering business — Food contamination, safety violations and regulatory penalties in the catering business would affect reputation and operations — the report notes elsewhere that food safety is renewal-critical, that clients audit against multiple standards and that lapses end contracts, against a base of over 300,000 meals a day. Mitigations stated: strict compliance with the FSS Act and all applicable food safety regulations, a centralised kitchen model enabling tighter quality control and consistency at scale, regular food safety audits and maintenance of necessary certifications.
- Control risk from geographically distributed, site-level operations — Not labelled a risk in the table but disclosed as the reason the control environment is designed the way it is: tens of thousands of people are deployed across client sites in every state and union territory, so the control environment leans heavily on technology and standardisation — defined SOPs at site level, digital capture of attendance, deployment and billing to reduce manual intervention and leakage, centralised procurement, payroll, statutory compliance and treasury, delegation-of-authority matrices and maker-checker controls over key financial processes. During the year the scope of controls testing was extended to the newly commissioned central kitchen and the expanded sourcing infrastructure.
- Client and end-market concentration / demand cyclicality in telecom — Disclosed as performance commentary rather than as a risk row: telecom spending by operators remained subdued for much of the year and capex spends by key players reduced, holding the Industrials & Telecom vertical to modest growth. The Company's stated mitigation is diversification — Vedang moving beyond telecom into satcom, fibre, data centres, telecom logistics and renewable energy networks, and Hofincons moving to higher-margin engineering-led contracts.

business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- Claims to be the ONLY player with this breadth of integrated infrastructure services, offering 'One partner across the entire infrastructure asset lifecycle - from manpower to engineering-led outcomes'.
- Six-vertical platform: Facility Management, Food Services, Security, Industrial & Power O&M, Telecom Networks and Talent Solutions, with a pan-India delivery footprint 'across all states and sectors, at operating scale few can replicate'.
- Frames its NSE & BSE listed, compliant platform as 'the structural winner as GST and labour codes formalise the industry'.
- Diversified revenue base on Q1 FY27 revenues: sector mix led by Industrials 31%, Commercial spaces 14%, Education 11%, BFSI 10%, Govt & Public Infra 10%, Telecom 8%, IT 7%, Healthcare 5%, Others 3%; client concentration Top 10 27%, Top 20 41%, Top 30 50%; zone mix South 41%, North 25%, East 18%, West 15%, International 1%.
- Strategy of 'Ascending the value chain' from SLA-based delivery to integrated commercial models that structurally enhance margins.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Acquisition - LSG] LSG India was founded in 2001, is currently owned by Aurelius Private Equity Fund (Germany) and was an erstwhile part of the Lufthansa Group; it operates in an oligopolistic market with high regulatory and entry barriers and long-term concessions until 2039.
- [Acquisition - STEAG] STEAG is an inorganic addition to the Smart Infra, Energy & Engineering segment contributing INR 76 Cr revenue for the quarter; the deck gives no consideration or ownership terms for it. Note the deck spells the name both 'STEAG' and 'STAEG' on the same slide.
- [Segment rename] 'Telecom and Industrials' was renamed 'Smart Infra, Energy and Engineering' with effect from 1 April 2026, so pre-April-2026 comparatives carry the old label.
- [Regulatory tailwind] Formalisation via GST and labour codes is claimed to be shifting share from unorganised operators to compliant national players, alongside client-led consolidation of vendors at national level.
- [Macro opportunity, sourced] Deck cites ~2/3 of facility management still in-house with the ratio expected to reverse by 2030; 87 MSF record office absorption in 2025; GCC count to reach 2,300 in 5 years from ~1,900; 40% urbanisation by 2030 from ~34%; manufacturing to contribute 17% of GDP vs 13% now; 30,000+ private hospital beds to be added (~$4bn capex); private educational institutions to grow to 3.8-4 lakh by 2030 from 3.2 lakh; thermal power to remain over 50% of generation for the mid-term (sources: CBRE, NASSCOM, Zinnov, FICCI & MoHFW, MOSPI ASI, MoE, IBEF, Knight Frank, Budget, Economic Survey, COAI).
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Bluspring delivers essential infrastructure support services that enable organisations to operate efficiently, safely and sustainably, spanning integrated facility management, institutional food and catering, industrial operations and maintenance, telecom network services, security services and a talent platform. It serves clients across commercial, industrial, healthcare, education, telecom, infrastructure and public-sector domains through an integrated service model built on a national workforce and technology-enabled processes. The Company was incorporated on 11 February 2024 as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Quess Corp Limited and became independent through a composite demerger scheme, listing on BSE and NSE on 11 June 2025.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Grow in two ways — strengthen the businesses built over the years, and pursue careful, disciplined acquisitions that complement them; invest only in businesses that strengthen existing capabilities, complement service offerings and deliver sustainable growth over time.
- Deepen cross-sell into the large base of single-service clients, particularly GCC, healthcare and BFSI accounts (stated priority for the coming year).
- Extend the technology capability to every new client relationship (stated priority for the coming year).
- Pursue further disciplined acquisitions (stated priority for the coming year).
- Restore profitability at foundit and create greater strategic value from the platform.
- Operate through a single integrated operating model — engineering, facilities management, food services, security, telecom infrastructure and talent solutions — as clients increasingly seek partners delivering multiple services with consistent standards and accountability.
- Keep India as the largest growth engine while pursuing international opportunities, using STEAG's capabilities to address power and industrial O&M demand in Africa and to explore Europe, the Middle East and other regions.
- Move to a more technology-led operating model, accelerate sales, reduce cost to serve and open new avenues of growth, while investing in talent and leadership.
- Diversify Vedang beyond telecom and shift Hofincons toward higher-margin engineering-led contracts, reinforced by the STEAG India acquisition.
- Build the organisation alongside scale — 'Embrace' diversity and inclusion programme launched, dedicated support for new and expectant mothers returning to work, and a zero-tolerance line on workplace safety.
- Ambition to set the benchmark for infrastructure services in India.
- No dividend is declared and no dividend distribution policy statement appears in the routed text — the block carrying the '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' heading actually contains website-disclosure and other-disclosure paragraphs from the Corporate Governance Report, so the Company's dividend intent cannot be read off this bundle (this is an absence in the routing, not a stated nil). What the text does state on capital structure and allocation: (1) the 2nd AGM notice puts a Special Resolution under Section 180(1)(c) to raise the Company's borrowing ceiling from an amount not exceeding Rs. 800 Crores to an amount not exceeding Rs. 1,300 Crores over and above paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium — i.e. headroom being created for debt-funded growth/acquisitions; (2) share-based rewards are used deliberately to attract and retain talent through two schemes — the Special Purpose Stock Ownership Plan 2025 (formulated 21 April 2025 under the Demerger Scheme, for grant of not more than 18,35,490 RSUs to employees who held QSOP 2020 options at Quess Corp and moved across, on terms not less favourable; 1,83,045 shares of Rs. 10 each were allotted during the year on RSU exercise per NRC approval of 3 February 2026) and the Employee Stock Option Scheme 2026, approved by shareholders through Postal Ballot on 23 April 2026 to grant performance-linked RSUs, build an ownership culture and retain managers; (3) governance discipline around capital — all FY26 related-party transactions were on an arm's length basis and in the ordinary course, none fell under Section 188(1) of the Act, none required shareholder approval, and the Company states it had no material related party transaction that may have potential conflict with its interests; the Audit Committee reviews RPTs quarterly under omnibus and prior approval, and reports are filed with the stock exchanges under Regulation 23(9); (4) internal financial controls were evaluated with no reportable material weakness or significant deficiency, and the statutory auditors issued unmodified opinions on both the financial statements and on internal financial controls; (5) the Company maintains an ERM framework aligned to COSO and ISO 31000 with a Risk Management Committee of Directors and senior management, a Board-approved Risk Management Policy, a Whistle Blower Policy and vigil mechanism, a Board Diversity Policy and an NRC-approved policy on director appointment, remuneration, succession and evaluation; (6) as an infrastructure management organisation the Company describes a relatively low direct environmental footprint and pursues energy/resource efficiency (paperless digitalisation, optimised HVAC settings, LED lighting, sensor-based water taps, a 'Switch Off When Not in Use' awareness initiative and investment in internal technology infrastructure) rather than capital-intensive environmental spend.
- Certifications maintained as a compliance and client-qualification requirement: ISO, PSARA and OHSAS across the business verticals (stated in the Regulatory & Licensing risk mitigation).
- Food safety governed by strict compliance with the FSS Act and applicable food safety regulations, with a centralised kitchen model for quality control, regular food safety audits and maintained certifications.
- Data protection framework aligned with the IT Act, Privacy Rules and the DPDP Act 2023, with regular security audits, timely system upgrades and periodic employee training on data privacy and cybersecurity.
- Enterprise Risk Management framework aligned with COSO and ISO 31000 principles, covering strategic, operational, financial, regulatory, compliance and sustainability-related risks, overseen by a dedicated Risk Management function and a Risk Management Committee comprising Directors and senior management, under a Board-approved Risk Management Policy published on the Company's website.
- Whistle Blower Policy and vigil mechanism in place under Section 177(9) of the Act and Regulation 22 of the Listing Regulations for reporting unethical behaviour, system violations, actual or suspected fraud or grave misconduct.
- Safety performance: the engineering / Hofincons business crossed 7.5 million man-hours without a single lost-time injury, under a stated zero-tolerance line on workplace safety; the Industrials & Telecom vertical delivered 25,000+ annual health and safety training hours during the year. (Stated in the CEO's message and Corporate Overview blocks, routed to other prompts in this bundle.)
- Diversity and inclusion: the 'Embrace' programme was launched during FY26, with dedicated support extended to new and expectant mothers returning to work; the Board has adopted a Board Diversity Policy covering thought, perspective, industry experience, geography, age, ethnicity, race and gender. (Partly from the CEO's message / Board's Report blocks routed to other prompts.)
- Environmental footprint characterised as relatively low and direct-operations-light; energy and resource initiatives during the year were digitalisation of business processes for paperless operations, optimised air-conditioning temperature settings, LED lighting across offices and operational facilities, sensor-based water taps, a 'Switch Off When Not in Use' awareness initiative and investment in internal technology infrastructure for resource optimisation. (Board's Report section 23, routed to the governance prompt.)
- Client-driven ESG as a commercial factor rather than a cost: occupiers and clients are writing measurable environmental and safety outcomes into service contracts — energy-performance-linked terms, smart metering and reporting on energy, water and waste — making demonstrated compliance a selection criterion; Hofincons' Digital Asset Management / EaaS line explicitly includes energy-as-a-service and ESG enablement.
- Formalisation of the workforce treated as a social outcome the Company is structurally positioned to deliver: the four Labour Codes in force from 21 November 2025 mandate written appointment letters, a statutory minimum wage, timely payment and extended social-security coverage, and the Company frames organised providers as the ones built to deliver these at scale.
- NO BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report) content was routed into this prompt — no emissions, energy, water, waste, LTIFR, gender-diversity, CSR-spend or grievance-redressal numbers are available in this bundle, so no quantified ESG target can be recorded.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Bluspring is an asset-light services business, so its expansion narrative is about acquisitions, footprint and platform build-out rather than plant capacity. The headline move of FY26 was the STEAG acquisition: in March 2026 the Company's subsidiary Bluspring New Horizon One Private Limited entered into a definitive agreement to acquire 100% of STEAG Energy Services India Private Limited for ₹180 crore in an all-cash deal. STEAG India, founded in 2001, is a wholly-owned subsidiary of STEAG Power GmbH (an 89-year-old German energy company) and is described as a market leader in power plant O&M, engineering services, digital solutions and management advisory for conventional and renewable power infrastructure, managing approximately 11.7 GW of power assets (including 600 MW in Africa) and 2,200 TPH of process steam supply capacity, with operations in India, South-East Asia, the Middle East and Africa, around 2,000 specialist professionals, roughly 90% of revenue from three-to-five-year annuity contracts, about USD 10 Mn of international revenue, cash of about ₹140 crore as of May 2026 and FY26 (unaudited) revenues of over ₹700 crore. The report states the STEAG acquisition added approximately 11.7 GW of managed power assets and world-class O&M capability to the industrial vertical, establishing it as one of the leading power services businesses in India. A second acquisition vehicle exists in the same structure — Bluspring New Horizon Two Private Limited — used for the LSG Sky Chefs India transaction referenced elsewhere in the report. In telecom, Vedang operates across 22 pan-India telecom circles in 67 geographies, with over 400 registered partners, executing more than 10,000 network deployment activities every month, and is positioning to capture emerging opportunities in satcom, fibre optics, data centres, telecom logistics and renewable energy networks — verticals the Company expects to see significant capital investment over the next three to five years. In the talent platform, foundit's FY27 roadmap is built around an eight-track AI Charter (intelligent parsing, semantic recruiter search, seeker discovery, AI-powered matching, data quality and internal automation), plus strategic B2B partnerships, a redesign of B2C seeker journeys and new upskilling lines of business, under a stated 'Build · Partner · Outsource' policy that reserves proprietary build for genuine differentiation. FY27 is positioned as a pivotal year for foundit, targeting aggressive sales growth and EBITDA profitability by Q4 FY27, including a targeted ~30% efficiency gain in finance operations. The report attributes the year's increase in depreciation and amortisation to operational capital expenditure incurred during the year, but gives no narrative capex programme, no plant/site commissioning schedule and no capex guidance number.

outlook.body:
- Management sees the market opportunity as structural rather than cyclical, citing the Labour Code tailwind, continued growth of Global Capability Centres in India, tightening ESG disclosure requirements, and structural growth of India's power sector — all favouring an organised, compliance-first operator.
- India's infrastructure build-out (metro rail, national highways, power generation over 505 GW installed, port capacity around 2,800 MTPA, more than 7.5 lakh telecom towers) is creating a much larger base of assets that will require professional operations and maintenance over the decades ahead.
- India's data centre industry is expanding rapidly with record capacity added during the year, and the addressable market is expected to reach US$90 billion between 2026 and 2035.
- Sustained public investment — highest-ever capital expenditure allocation of ₹12.2 lakh crore in the Union Budget FY27 — reaffirms infrastructure as central to the growth agenda.
- Demand for reliable facility management, operations, maintenance, compliance and safety services will grow as India's infrastructure base expands, extending beyond public infrastructure into metals and mining, power generation, speciality chemicals and petrochemicals where critical-asset performance depends on efficient O&M.
- Growth drivers named by the CEO: organic cross-selling across the client base, Vedang's diversification beyond telecom, and Hofincons' shift toward higher-margin engineering-led contracts, now reinforced by the STEAG India acquisition.
- Three drivers behind FY26 improvement: new client wins, strengthening relationships with existing clients, and improving operational efficiency across the business.
- Telecom spending by operators remained subdued for much of the year, holding Telecom & Industrials growth to a more modest level; the Industrials sub-vertical grew strongly at higher margins.
- Clients increasingly buy integrated solutions rather than standalone services, making the Company a strategic partner; compliance and safety record matters enormously in regulated sectors; real-time dashboards, automated compliance tracking and predictive capabilities give clients continuous live visibility, helping retention.
- Recent acquisitions beginning to contribute plus continuing operational improvements are the stated basis for improving returns.
- 164 new contracts mobilised during FY26, representing an annual contract value of ₹459 crore.
- 95% of clients retained in FY26, across more than 1,000 organisations spanning ten sectors.
- No formal order book / pipeline value (closing order book, L1 position or book-to-bill) is disclosed in the routed text.

risks.note: Bluspring is a people-intensive, multi-site service business managing roughly 93,000 people across client sites, so difficulty in recruiting, training and retaining qualified personnel, or high attrition rates, could disrupt operations and increase costs. Mitigations stated: investment in a robust people supply chain backed by recruitment, onboarding and training programmes; benchmarked compensation models and focused retention strategies to reduce attrition and ensure operational continuity.
risks.risk: Workforce management risk — recruiting, training and retaining qualified personnel; high attrition

risks.note: Negative cash flows and working capital requirements can impact operations and the ability to meet short-term obligations — structurally acute in an outsourced services model where wages are paid ahead of client collections. Mitigations stated: diversified revenue streams across multiple service lines to reduce dependency on any single vertical; tightly managed collections and credit control; prioritising cash-generating contracts and segments; and strategic partnerships to optimise working capital cycles.
risks.risk: Working capital and cash flow risk

risks.note: Stringent labour regulations and compliance requirements across multiple states carry potential penalties for non-compliance. This is doubly structural for Bluspring: the four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, and the report elsewhere attributes the year's exceptional items primarily to the estimated one-time impact of adopting the new labour code (higher provision towards retiral benefits) — so the same regulation is both the Company's tailwind and its largest compliance exposure. Mitigations stated: in-house legal and compliance teams enforcing standardised processes, regular field-team training on labour law updates, and proactive engagement with regulatory authorities.
risks.risk: Labour law compliance risk across multiple states

risks.note: Multiple licences and approvals are required across the different business verticals (facility management, catering, security, telecom, industrial O&M), and suspension or non-renewal of a critical permit would halt delivery. Mitigations stated: a centralised regulatory tracking system with domain-specific legal expertise per vertical; proactive application, timely renewal and close monitoring of all statutory licences; periodic internal compliance audits; and maintenance of all critical certifications including ISO, PSARA and OHSAS to meet client and regulatory expectations.
risks.risk: Regulatory and licensing risk — suspension or non-renewal of critical permits

risks.note: Risks related to data breaches, cyber-attacks and non-compliance with evolving data protection regulations including the DPDP Act 2023 — material given the Company runs digital workforce, attendance and billing platforms and a talent marketplace holding job-seeker data. Mitigations stated: a data protection framework aligned with the IT Act, Privacy Rules and the DPDP Act; continuous strengthening of security infrastructure through regular audits and timely system upgrades; and periodic employee training on data privacy and cybersecurity protocols.
risks.risk: Data privacy and cybersecurity risk, including DPDP Act 2023 compliance

risks.note: Food contamination, safety violations and regulatory penalties in the catering business would affect reputation and operations — the report notes elsewhere that food safety is renewal-critical, that clients audit against multiple standards and that lapses end contracts, against a base of over 300,000 meals a day. Mitigations stated: strict compliance with the FSS Act and all applicable food safety regulations, a centralised kitchen model enabling tighter quality control and consistency at scale, regular food safety audits and maintenance of necessary certifications.
risks.risk: Food safety and quality risk in the catering business

risks.note: Not labelled a risk in the table but disclosed as the reason the control environment is designed the way it is: tens of thousands of people are deployed across client sites in every state and union territory, so the control environment leans heavily on technology and standardisation — defined SOPs at site level, digital capture of attendance, deployment and billing to reduce manual intervention and leakage, centralised procurement, payroll, statutory compliance and treasury, delegation-of-authority matrices and maker-checker controls over key financial processes. During the year the scope of controls testing was extended to the newly commissioned central kitchen and the expanded sourcing infrastructure.
risks.risk: Control risk from geographically distributed, site-level operations

risks.note: Disclosed as performance commentary rather than as a risk row: telecom spending by operators remained subdued for much of the year and capex spends by key players reduced, holding the Industrials & Telecom vertical to modest growth. The Company's stated mitigation is diversification — Vedang moving beyond telecom into satcom, fibre, data centres, telecom logistics and renewable energy networks, and Hofincons moving to higher-margin engineering-led contracts.
